Build & deployment::Monorepo usage.summary: Share common environment variables across monorepo packages by defining them in a reusable preset and extending that preset from each package. The `extends` property combines shared configuration with package-specific environment definitions.
Build & deployment::Monorepo usage.explanation: Define shared environment variables once in a preset package, then let each package extend that preset with the `extends` property. This keeps common validation centralized while allowing individual applications to add their own server or client variables.

parameters.name: env
parameters.description: An environment configuration object whose `extends` property references one or more reusable presets.

Build & deployment::Monorepo usage.returns: An environment object containing the inherited preset configuration together with the consuming package's definition.

useCases.scenario: A deployment platform provides environment variables used by multiple packages.

keyPoints: Use `extends` on an environment definition to inherit variables from another preset.
Presets can also bring in deployment-provider system variables alongside shared package variables.
A shared preset is suitable when several monorepo packages use the same environment variables.
gotchas: The shared definition must be supplied as a preset and included through the `extends` property.
Use this pattern for variables shared by multiple packages in a monorepo; package-specific variables still belong in the consuming package.

Build & deployment::Per-environment valu.summary: Keep one validated environment-variable schema while supplying distinct values for development, preview, and production deployments. T3 Env also separates server-only variables from values exposed to client code.
Build & deployment::Per-environment valu.explanation: Define one environment-variable schema for the application, then provide environment-specific values through the deployment environment or separate environment files. T3 Env validates the supplied values against that schema and exposes them through the generated, type-safe environment object while keeping server-only values away from client code.
Build & deployment::Per-environment valu.returns: A type-safe environment object containing validated server and, when configured, client variables.

example.explanation: Use separate environment files so the same variable name resolves to the configuration appropriate for each deployment environment.

useCases.scenario: Preview deployments

useCases.title: Supply production secrets and service endpoints through the deployment environment.
useCases.scenario: Production

keyPoints: Create a schema once and validate the values supplied by each deployment environment.
After defining the schema, consume the validated environment object instead of reading untyped process variables throughout the application.
Schema validators can supply defaults when a variable is intentionally optional in a particular environment.
Server-only variables are protected from client exposure, and accidental client access produces a diagnostic failure.
gotchas: Environment values arrive as strings; begin validation with a string schema before transforming or coercing them.
Do not assume server variables are available in browser code; T3 Env keeps them server-side.

Build & deployment::Skipping validation.summary: T3 Env can conditionally bypass environment validation, including during Docker builds where secrets are unavailable. Use this deliberately because skipped checks can desynchronize types from runtime values.
Build & deployment::Skipping validation.explanation: Set `skipValidation` to a condition that is true only for the intended container build. When active, T3 Env bypasses validation for both the declared environment variables and extended presets, which can allow a Docker image to build without runtime secrets; normal runs should keep validation enabled.

parameters.name: skipValidation
parameters.description: A boolean condition; when true, T3 Env skips validation.

Build & deployment::Skipping validation.returns: An environment configuration created by createEnv, with validation conditionally bypassed.

example.title: Skip validation during a deliberate Docker build
example.explanation: This enables the documented opt-out only when the Docker build flag is set and no required variables are available.

useCases.scenario: A Docker image build does not have all runtime environment variables available.

useCases.title: Lint-time configuration
useCases.scenario: Linting or a similar process loads configuration without the deployment environment.

useCases.title: Deferred secret injection
useCases.scenario: A deliberate build pipeline stage must create an artifact before runtime secrets are injected.

keyPoints: Use the option for linting-like contexts or other deliberate situations where validation cannot run.
A supported scenario is a Docker image build that intentionally lacks some environment variables.
Configure `skipValidation` with a boolean condition rather than treating it as a permanent global bypass.
gotchas: Do not use this as a general workaround: skipping checks can make the declared types disagree with actual runtime values.
The opt-out applies to extended presets as well as the environment variables defined in the current configuration.

Defining the schema::Client variables.summary: Declare only browser-safe environment values in the client schema, and give them the framework’s required public prefix. T3 Env enforces that prefix in both types and runtime validation.
Defining the schema::Client variables.explanation: Client variables are the subset of environment values intended for browser code. Declare only publishable values in the client schema and configure clientPrefix to match the framework’s required exposure prefix; T3 Env checks that the names comply with this prefix at both the type and runtime levels.

parameters.name: clientPrefix
parameters.description: Prefix required on every key in the client schema; it must match the framework’s client-side exposure convention.

parameters.name: client
parameters.description: Schema entries for values that may be exposed to client-side code; each key must use clientPrefix.

Defining the schema::Client variables.returns: A validated environment object containing the declared client variables.

useCases.scenario: Keep secrets out of the client schema while exposing non-sensitive configuration.

keyPoints: Choose the client prefix from the framework’s client-exposure convention before defining the schema.
clientPrefix configures the required beginning of every client variable name.
The correct prefix depends on the framework; Astro uses PUBLIC_, whereas Vite uses VITE_.
T3 Env validates the required prefix during type checking and when the environment is processed.
The client section contains publishable values validated with the chosen schema library.
gotchas: Every key in the client schema must begin with the configured clientPrefix; otherwise TypeScript rejects the schema.
Prefix compliance is checked twice, so an invalid client variable is not merely a compile-time concern.

Defining the schema::createEnv.summary: Declare and validate server and client environment variables in one schema. createEnv returns typed access to the validated values.
Defining the schema::createEnv.explanation: createEnv combines server-only and client-exposed variable schemas, checks client names against a required prefix, and validates values from the configured runtime environment. The returned env object provides typed, validated access to those variables.

parameters.description: Schemas for server-only environment variables.

parameters.name: clientPrefix
parameters.description: Required prefix for client-side variable names.

parameters.name: client
parameters.description: Schemas for variables available to client-side code.

parameters.name: runtimeEnv
parameters.description: Runtime object containing environment values, typically process.env or import.meta.env.

Defining the schema::createEnv.returns: A typed env object containing validated environment variables.

example.explanation: This defines validated server and client variables, requires client names to use the PUBLIC_ prefix, and reads values from process.env.

keyPoints: Call createEnv with an object containing the environment variable schemas.
clientPrefix declares the required prefix for variables exposed to client code.
runtimeEnv specifies the source object from which values are read, commonly process.env or import.meta.env.
Schemas can use any validator implementing Standard Schema, not only Zod.
Use the returned env object throughout the application for typed access and editor completion.
gotchas: If the application has no client-side variables, omit both client-related properties.
clientPrefix is checked during typing and runtime validation, so client variable names must follow it.

Defining the schema::Server variables.summary: Define secrets and other backend-only values in the `server` schema. Omit `clientPrefix` and `client` when the variables should exist only on the server.
Defining the schema::Server variables.explanation: Place secrets and other backend-only values in the server schema passed to createEnv. Omitting client configuration keeps those variables unavailable to client code; if variable names are sensitive, split the schemas so their validation definitions are not shipped to the browser.
Defining the schema::Server variables.syntax: createEnv({ server: { VARIABLE_NAME: validator }, runtimeEnv: process.env })

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Object containing server-only environment variable validators; clientPrefix and client are omitted for a server-only schema.

Defining the schema::Server variables.returns: An env object exposing validated, type-safe environment variables; server variables are unavailable in client code.

keyPoints: Use only the server schema when every defined variable must remain server-side.
Client exposure is controlled separately by a required framework-specific prefix; server variables do not use that client prefix.
The library prevents server variable values from entering the client bundle.
A proxy and safe parsing allow validation to work without exposing server values to client code.
Declare each backend-only variable under server and attach an appropriate validator.
gotchas: A combined schema is convenient, but its server validation schemas are shipped to the client; split the schemas if variable names are sensitive.
Do not access server variables from client code: they are unavailable there and access attempts throw an error.

Defining the schema::Shared variables.summary: Define environment-variable schemas for server and client use with createEnv. Declare shared values in the appropriate schema, and require a framework-specific prefix for variables exposed to the browser.
Defining the schema::Shared variables.explanation: T3 Env uses separate server and client schema sections to describe which environment variables the application may use. Put values needed by server code in server, and put browser-safe values in client with the framework’s required prefix; runtimeEnv supplies the actual environment object to validate.

parameters.name: clientPrefix

parameters.name: client

Defining the schema::Type inference.summary: Validate environment variables with a schema, then derive Node's ProcessEnv type from that schema. This provides autocomplete and type checking while consuming the validated names.
Defining the schema::Type inference.explanation: Define a validation schema, parse the environment values, and extend Node's ProcessEnv interface with the schema's inferred type. This enables editor autocomplete and type checking, but the runtime values on process.env remain the original strings, so transforms can make the declared types inaccurate.
Defining the schema::Type inference.returns: The documentation describes a type augmentation rather than a runtime-returning helper; the schema parse validates process.env.

The augmentation makes schema-defined environment names available to autocomplete across the application.
Parse process.env with the schema before relying on the declared environment-variable types.
Extend ProcessEnv with the validator's inferred schema type.

Avoid transforms when augmenting ProcessEnv unless the runtime string values and inferred types intentionally match.

Validation rules::Cross-field refinement.summary: Use createFinalSchema to add cross-field validation to T3 Env. This lets one environment variable become required when another has a selected value.
Validation rules::Cross-field refinement.explanation: Use createFinalSchema to apply a validator-level refinement after the generated environment schema. This is the appropriate place to inspect multiple environment variables together and add a targeted validation issue for the dependent variable.

parameters.description: Environment schema configuration containing the server-side variable definitions and a createFinalSchema callback.

The validator used for the final schema can follow the Standard Schema interface supported by T3 Env.
Define the raw environment variables with string-aware validators before refining their combined values.
The schema can use a supported validator library and its refinement capabilities rather than being limited to one validator implementation.
gotchas: The refinement must be supplied through createFinalSchema; the page documents this option for applying additional refinement or transformation.
Environment values arrive as strings, so account for string input before applying parsing, coercion, or cross-field checks.

Validation rules::Defaults.summary: Use validator defaults only when the fallback is genuinely safe. If an environment variable may be an empty string, enable emptyStringAsUndefined so the default can apply when the value is effectively absent.
Validation rules::Defaults.explanation: Defaults are supplied through the validator schema, but an empty environment value can prevent them from taking effect. Enable emptyStringAsUndefined when empty strings should behave like missing values, then use a default only for a value with a safe fallback such as a local development domain.

parameters.name: runtimeEnv
parameters.description: Runtime values supplied to the environment schema.

parameters.name: emptyStringAsUndefined
parameters.description: Converts empty strings to undefined before validation when enabled.

Validation rules::Defaults.returns: A validated environment object whose values reflect the validator schemas and their defaults.

keyPoints: Defaults are defined with the validator you choose, because T3 Env supports the validator’s standard features.
An empty environment value can interfere with a schema default, so decide explicitly whether empty strings should count as missing.
Set emptyStringAsUndefined to true when empty strings should be converted to undefined before validation.
The exact default declaration depends on the validator, while T3 Env passes the schema behavior through.
gotchas: An empty string is not the same as a missing value: for a string field with a default, an explicitly empty environment variable bypasses the default unless emptyStringAsUndefined is enabled.

Validation rules::Error messages.summary: T3 Env lets you customize schema-validation failures through onValidationError. The callback receives validation issues so you can report the invalid variable and what its schema expected.
Validation rules::Error messages.explanation: T3 Env passes failed schema validation issues to the onValidationError callback, allowing applications to report which environment variable failed and inspect the expected validation details.

parameters.description: Validation problems supplied by the validator, including details about the failed variable and rule.

keyPoints: Use onValidationError to receive validation issues after the environment schema rejects one or more values.
The callback receives an issues array that can be logged to identify the invalid variable and the validation problem.
The callback accepts Standard Schema issue objects, providing a consistent error-reporting shape across supported validators.
After reporting the issues, the callback can throw an application-specific error to stop startup or the build.
gotchas: The callback runs only after schema validation has failed; it is not a general environment-variable access hook.
Values are passed directly to the validator by default, so validator-specific type errors can appear in the reported issues.

Validation rules::Format validation.summary: Use Standard Schema validators to constrain environment variables such as URLs and ports instead of accepting arbitrary strings. T3 Env supports compatible libraries including Zod, Valibot, ArkType, and Typia.
Validation rules::Format validation.explanation: Define each environment variable with a Standard Schema validator instead of accepting an unrestricted string. T3 Env passes runtime values to the chosen validator, so URL formats, numeric port bounds, and permitted enum values are checked when the environment is parsed.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Environment schema configuration passed to createEnv, including server variables and runtime values.

keyPoints: Use any validator library that implements Standard Schema, rather than being limited to one validation library.
Schemas validate environment input at runtime before your application relies on it.
Use a URL validator for variables that must contain a URL instead of an arbitrary string.
Coerce numeric environment values when the application expects a number; add range constraints when needed.
Standard Schema v1-compatible validators can provide the constraints used by T3 Env.

Validation rules::Required versus option.summary: T3 Env treats schema entries as required unless their validator is marked optional. Use `.optional()` only for values that may be absent, so missing requirements fail validation instead of being silently defaulted.
Validation rules::Required versus option.explanation: Define required variables with a non-optional validator so validation fails when the value is missing. Add `.optional()` only when absence is valid; this keeps the schema and runtime values aligned instead of silently supplying a default.
Validation rules::Required versus option.syntax: createEnv({ server, client?, clientPrefix?, runtimeEnv?, runtimeEnvStrict?, emptyStringAsUndefined? })

keyPoints: Server-only variables are not exposed to client code; client access produces an error rather than a usable value.
A required variable can use a non-empty string validator, such as `z.string().min(1)`.

gotchas: Values are passed directly to the validator by default, so an empty string is not automatically treated as an absent value.
If your environment supplies empty strings for omitted values, enable `emptyStringAsUndefined` when that behavior is intended.

Validation rules::Transformations.summary: Transform environment-variable strings into application types at the validation boundary. The recipes show explicit boolean transforms and number parsing with a follow-up number check, plus Zod number coercion.
Validation rules::Transformations.explanation: Environment variables arrive as strings, so begin with a string validator and then transform or coerce them into the types used by the application. Number conversion can use parsing followed by a number check; boolean conversion should use explicit application rules rather than generic primitive coercion.
Validation rules::Transformations.syntax: createEnv({ server: { KEY: z.string().transform(...).pipe(...) }, runtimeEnv: process.env })

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Environment schema configuration passed to createEnv, including server validators and runtimeEnv.

Validation rules::Transformations.returns: A typed, validated environment object with transformed values.
